content.body: Finding all possible subsets of a set is a classic problem with many applications. Today, we'll learn how to generate all subsets efficiently using a backtracking approach. You'll implement a solution that builds subsets step by step.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain the backtracking approach to generating subsets
2. Implement a recursive function to build all subsets
3. Visualize the decision tree for subset generation
4. Handle base cases in recursive subset generation
5. Return all subsets in the required format
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a small example. Given the array [1, 2], what are all possible subsets? Think about including or excluding each element.
content.title: Try it

content.body: Now let's try with three elements. Given [1, 2, 3], how many subsets should there be? Remember, each element can be either included or excluded.
content.title: Try a bigger array
content.successMessage: Exactly! With 3 elements, we have 2³ = 8 subsets.

content.body: Notice how subsets grow exponentially. For [1, 2, 3], can you think of a systematic way to generate all subsets without missing any?
content.title: Pattern recognition
content.prompt: What's a method to systematically generate subsets?
content.successMessage: Good thinking! We can use a decision tree where at each element, we choose to include it or exclude it.

content.body: You manually listed subsets by considering each element's inclusion/exclusion. This is essentially what our algorithm will do systematically. For small arrays, manual listing works, but we need a method that scales.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has 10 elements, there are 1,024 subsets. Manually listing them is impractical. We need an algorithmic approach that can handle any size. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The key insight is that generating subsets is like walking through a decision tree. At each element, we have two choices: include it or exclude it. We need to explore all possible paths through this tree.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step. For subsets, we're keeping track of our current path (the subset we're building) and exploring all branches.

content.body: We'll use backtracking: start with an empty subset, then for each element, make two recursive calls - one including the element, one excluding it. When we reach the end of the array, we save the current subset.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample: For [1, 2, 3]: Start with []. At index 0: include 1 → [1], exclude 1 → []. From [1]: at index 1: include 2 → [1,2], exclude 2 → [1]. Continue this process to generate all 8 subsets.

content.body:
1. Create a result array to store all subsets
2. Create a current subset array to track the current path
3. Define a recursive function that takes an index parameter
4. Base case: if index equals array length, add current subset to result
5. Recursive case: 
   a. Include the current element, then recurse with index+1
   b. Exclude the current element (pop if included), then recurse with index+1
6. Start recursion with index 0
7. Return the result array
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function skeleton
steps.instruction: Create the function skeleton that takes an array nums and returns all subsets. Initialize the result array and current subset array.
steps.hint: You'll need two arrays: one to store all subsets (result) and one to track the current subset being built.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function should be defined with empty result and current arrays
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the basic structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure to initialize both arrays.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember we need two arrays: one for all results, one for current subset.

steps.title: Define the recursive helper
steps.instruction: Inside the subsets function, define a recursive helper function called backtrack that takes an index parameter.
steps.hint: The helper function will be called recursively to explore include/exclude decisions.
steps.expectedOutcome: backtrack function defined with index parameter
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Now we have our recursive helper ready.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure backtrack takes an index parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to define a function called backtrack that takes index as a parameter.

steps.title: Implement the base case
steps.instruction: Inside the backtrack function, add the base case: when index equals nums.length, push a copy of current to result and return.
steps.hint: Use slice() or spread operator [...] to create a copy of current array before pushing to result.
steps.expectedOutcome: Base case that adds current subset copy to result when at end of array
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! The base case handles when we've processed all elements.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Remember to push a copy, not the reference, and return.
steps.feedbackWrong: Base case should check if index === nums.length, then push current.slice() to result and return.

steps.title: Include the current element
steps.instruction: After the base case, implement the 'include' branch: push nums[index] to current, then call backtrack(index + 1).
steps.hint: This represents choosing to include the current element in our subset.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that pushes current element to current and recurses
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! This branch includes the current element.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Make sure to push nums[index] then call backtrack(index + 1).
steps.feedbackWrong: The include branch should be: current.push(nums[index]); backtrack(index + 1);

steps.title: Exclude the current element
steps.instruction: After the include branch, implement the 'exclude' branch: pop from current (to undo the include), then call backtrack(index + 1).
steps.hint: This represents choosing NOT to include the current element. We need to remove what we added in the include branch.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that pops from current and recurses without including element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now we have both include and exclude branches.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good. Remember to pop() from current before the exclude recursive call.
steps.feedbackWrong: The exclude branch should be: current.pop(); backtrack(index + 1);

steps.title: Start recursion and return result
steps.instruction: After defining backtrack, call backtrack(0) to start the recursion, then return result at the end of subsets function.
steps.hint: We need to initiate the recursion with the first index (0) and return the final result array.
steps.expectedOutcome: Complete function that starts recursion and returns all subsets
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've implemented the complete subsets algorithm!
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost done. Call backtrack(0) and return result.
steps.feedbackWrong: After defining backtrack, add: backtrack(0); return result;

content.body:
Congratulations! You've implemented the subsets algorithm using backtracking. Key takeaways:
1. Subsets generation is a decision tree problem
2. Backtracking explores all include/exclude choices
3. We use a current array to track the path and result to collect all subsets
4. The time complexity is O(2ⁿ) since we generate 2ⁿ subsets
5. Remember to create copies when saving subsets to avoid reference issues
content.title: Done
